3 key points

Google Labs is testing Stitch Loop, a product-maintenance agent that turns live product signals and a team’s measurable goals into proposed software changes. It can keep tracking results and suggest follow-up work, but code changes remain ordinary GitHub pull requests that people must review before merging. The experiment broadens Stitch beyond interface creation toward ongoing product improvement; access starts through a global waitlist, with Google AI Ultra users prioritized.

1. 01 It watches what you connectA repository supplies the implementation. Logs, behavior data, feedback and product documents can help explain what users experience.
2. 02 It proposes a direction before writing the fixSuggestions cite evidence. Once you choose a solution, Loop writes code in an isolated cloud sandbox and opens a GitHub pull request.
3. 03 The measurement still needs an ownerA change in traffic mix alone can cause a 12-point checkout decline. Define the denominator, the segments and the outcome before choosing a fix.
4. 04 Access starts with a global waitlistAnyone can join the list. Eligible Google AI Ultra users receive priority. Google’s launch gives no general-release date or per-loop price.

## 01 — InputsGive the agent a question it can answer [...] A checkout dashboard goes from 87% completion to 75%. Someone needs to find out whether the page broke, a campaign brought in different customers, or the analytics changed. Google Stitch Loop can take that question to a connected codebase, suggest an explanation and prepare a fix. The most valuable response may be to leave the code alone.

In its November 18 launch, Google Labs describes a long-running product agent for software that already has users. You give it a standing objective, connect GitHub and supply the evidence it needs. Two decisions stay with the team. Someone chooses which proposed solution is worth building, and someone reviews the resulting pull request before it merges. As of November 19, Google is accepting waitlist registrations.Google Labs’ Stitch Loop announcement [...] Google also describes using Loop from Slack or as a source of persistent product context for coding agents such as Antigravity. The Stitch CLI and MCP make that context available to another agent. In Slack, the documented uses for @stitch include daily insight digests and creating loops. Daily refers to the digest. Google gives no fixed interval between samples of a production metric.

If another agent can consume the same context, decide which repository each agent may change and who owns the resulting requests. A developer responding to a digest should be able to find the original insight and discover whether a fix is already in review. Ourguide to managing agents on GitHub covers how to keep those reviews visible when more than one agent contributes.

Each cycle operates independently, allowing the agent to work on multiple optimization paths simultaneously. When Stitch Loop detects a metric decline or identifies a potential improvement, it generates a code proposal complete with context about the issue and expected impact. The agent then monitors whether the proposed change achieves the desired outcome, creating a feedback loop that informs future suggestions.

## Human Review Requirements [...] # Google Stitch Loop: Always-On Agent Rewrites Code 24/7

Google Labs officially launched Stitch Loop on November 18, 2026, introducing a continuous agent that connects directly to codebases and live product metrics to identify issues, propose fixes, and write code around the clock. Unlike traditional development tools that complete a task and terminate, Stitch Loop operates indefinitely, monitoring deployed software to prevent performance regressions even after initial objectives are met.

## How Stitch Loop Works [...] ## Integration With Antigravity

Stitch Loop functions as a service layer for Google's Antigravity platform, accessible through the Stitch CLI, MCP protocol, and Slack @-mentions. This architecture allows development teams to trigger optimization cycles from multiple interfaces without switching tools. The integration with Antigravity positions Stitch Loop as part of Google's broader developer tooling ecosystem rather than a standalone product.

Teams can configure Stitch Loop to monitor specific repositories, set priority metrics, and define thresholds that trigger new optimization cycles. The agent operates asynchronously, queuing suggestions and updates that developers can review during normal workflow rather than demanding immediate attention.
